# S1M-1 2.1.1 Converting Integer to Binary

## 2.1.1 Converting Integer to Binary

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

- **Computer**
- A computer is a programmable device that stores, retrieves, and processes data.

-2 main architectures of computers:

1.Von-Neumann

2. Harvard

- **Binary System**
- Everything in the Binary System is 1 and 0.

**Bit**

-the smallest unit in the Binary System

-either a 1 or a 0

**Byte**

-8 bits

  - **Binary Operations**
- **Most Significant Byte/Bit**
- **-**the byte/bit that contributes the most to the value. Think of digit 1, the hundreds digit, in 123

**Least Significant Byte/Bit**

-the byte/bit that contributes the least to the value. Think of the digit 3, the ones digit, in 123

-repeatedly divide the number by 2

-record the remainder of each division

-continue until the quotient reaches 0

-read the remainder from bottom to top to obtain the binary number.

## 2.1.2 Converting Binary to Integer

-assign powers of 2 to each digit, starting from 20 on the right

-multiply each digit by its corresponding power of 2

-add the results.

$${11001}_{2}=16+8+0+0+1={25}_{10}$$

## 2.1.3 Converting Real Number to Binary

-separate its integer and fractional parts

-convert the integer part using repeated division by 2

-for the fractional part, repeatedly multiply by 2 and record the integer part of each result.

-read these digits from top to bottom

-finally, combine both parts using a binary point.

$${10.625}_{10}={1010.101}_{2}$$

Some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly with a finite number of binary digits and must be truncated or rounded.

**Truncation**

This is a method that simply cuts the binary expression into limited digits.

$${0.10101101}_{2}\to {0.1010}_{2}$$

**Round-Off**

Round-off is a method used to approximate a binary number to a fixed number of digits.

If the first discarded bit is **0**, the retained bits remain unchanged

If it is **1**, add 1 to the last retained bit, carrying to the left if necessary.

$${0.10101101}_{2}\to {0.1011}_{2}$$

## 2.1.4 Converting Binary to Real Number

-assign powers of 2 to each digit:

digits to the left of the binary point use non-negative powers of 2

digits to the right use negative powers of 2

-multiply each digit by its corresponding power and add the results.

$${101.011}_{2}=4+1+0.25+0.125$$

## 2.2 Two’s Complement Notation

- a method used by computers to represent positive and negative integers

-In an n-bit two’s complement number:

0 as the first bit indicates non-negative number

1 as the first bit indicates negative number

**Converting integers to binary**

If the integer is non-negative, the two’s complement notation of it is simply in section 2.1.1

If the integer is negative, do the following process:

Eg: Convert -3 into two’s complement

True Form: 1|0000011

One’s Complement: 1|1111100 invert

Two’s Complement: 1|1111101 add 1

or, the formula way:

$$\text{Two's Complement}={2}^{n}-\left| x \right|$$

Two’s complement of -5 = 28 – 5 = 251D = 11111011B

and it’s reverse function, to convert a two’s complement binary number into the integer it represents:

$$x=\left\{ \begin{matrix}B, & \text{if MSB}=0 \\ B-{2}^{n}, & \text{if MSB}=1\end{matrix} \right.$$

MSB = Most significant bit (first bit of the expression)

B = the decimal value of the two’s complement notation

x = 11111011B – 256D = 251D – 256D = -5D

-Note that the two’s complement can store numbers in the range of -2n-1 to 2n-1 -1

-Any operation that involves more bits to store will cause an **Overflow**

## 2.3 Numbers and Memory

## 2.3.1 Overflow

-This is a situation where a calculated value cannot fit in to the number of digits reserved for it:

127D + 5D in 8 bits will cause an overflow since 132D is out of the range

## 2.3.2 Floating Point Numbers

-scientific notation: written in the form of a * 10b where 1<= a < 10

-Similarly, a floating point number consists of 3 parts: The **Sign**, **Mantissa**, and **Exponent.**

The difference is that they are expressed in binaries and the mantissa a is 0<=a<1

-The decimal number 12.5 converted to floating point is:

| **Description** | **Sign** | **Mantissa** | **Exponent** | **Expression** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Convert 12.5 to binary | **0** | 1100.1B |  |  |
| Move the decimal place 4 steps left so that the mantissa is less than 1 | **0** | 0.11001B | 100B | 0.11001 * 2100 |
| Keep only franctional part of mantissa and concatenate in to a stream of bits | **0** | 11001B | 0100B | 0110010100 |

**-Converting floating point number to decimal numbers:**

-1: put the mantissa into a fractional part. 11001B -> 0.11001B

-2: move the decimal place 100B steps right. 0.1100B -> 1100.1B

-3: convert to decimal. 1100.1B -> 12.5D

Note that this encoding method is only class convention and isn’t the real method.

## 2.4 Binary Arithmetic

**3. Data**

-Data refers to the symbols that represent facts, objects, and ideas.

becomes information when it’s presented in a format that people can understand and use

Computers and digital devices can work with numbers, text, symbols, images, video, audio, etc.

- **Data representation** refers to the form in which data is sorted, processed and transmitted.

## 3.1 Analog Data

-Analog data refers to the type of data with continuous values and represented with infinity scales of value

Eg: Sound, Color, Audio (in the real life)

## 3.2 Digital Data

-Digital data uses discrete values.

Represented using bits.

Eg: a switch (on and off)

**4. Text Representation**

**Character**

-Composed of letters, symbols, and numerals that will not be used in arithmatic operations

-Digital computers typically represent character data using **ASCII**

# S1M-2 4.1 ASCII

## 4.1 ASCII

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

-Stands for the “American Standard Code for Information Interchange”

-ASCII employes a 7-bit binary code to represent 128 unique characters, enabling the encoding of English letters, digits, and punctuation.

## 4.2 ANSI

-The ANSI encoding system is an extension of ASCII.

-It is a local encoding system, meaning that each country uses a different set of values.

-ANSI encoding system extends the range to 65536 values.

-The first 128 values of ANSI encoding system is same as ASCII

-Shortcoming: Conflicts between different languages

## 4.3 Unicode

Provides a comprehensive system to represent characters from all writing systems through variable-width encodings.

It is a big set of values that stores every character in every language

**Downward compatible** with ASCII

Each character has its unique code

## 4.3.1 UTF

-UTF stands for Unicode Transformation Format

-There are different standards of UTF, such as UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32

-The length for representing each character in UTF-8 can differ

1-byte represents only English

2-byte represents latin-script languages

3-byte represents mostly Asian languages (Chinese)

4-byte represents everything else

**BOM(Byte order mark)**

-The byte order mark is a actual unicode character U+FEFF

-Its size: however many bytes U+FEFF takes in that encoding

(2 for UTF-16, 3 for UTF-8, 4 for UTF-32).

-BOM is discouraged for UTF-8 (Default: No BOM for UTF-8)

**Big-endian & Little-endian**

-These are two arrangements of different bytes

Big endian: put the most significant byte first

Little endian: put the least significant byte first

Eg: “A” = 00 41 under UTF-16

The big end is the byte “00”

The little end is the byte “41”

“A” in BE order is 00 41

“A” in LE order is 41 00

**5. Audio Representation**

**Sound**

-Sound is an **analog** signal; therefore, we’ll have to convert it into digital signal to use to in computer

-This allows the computer to store audio and convert it back to analog signal whenever the user wants to play in

-There are three stages to convert:

## 5.1 Sampling

-This process discretizes the signal in the time domain by capturing snapshots at fixed intervals

The smaller the fixed interval, the more accurate the reproduction is

**Nyquist Theorem** states that the sampling frequency must be greater than **twice** the signal to perfectly reconstruct the original sound

- **Image Representation**
- A digital image is a representation of a picture using binary data.
- Raster images are divided into small units called pixels, and each pixel stores information describing its colour or brightness.
- A computer reconstructs the image by displaying these pixels in their correct positions.

# S1M-3 6.1 Pixels and Resolution

## 6.1 Pixels and Resolution

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

-A **pixel** (picture element) is the smallest individually addressable element of a raster image.

Each pixel contains a value that determines the color displayed at that position.

-Resolution describes the number of pixels in an image, usually expressed as width × height. An image measuring 1920 × 1080 has 1920 pixels in each row and 1080 rows.

Eg: Total pixels = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels.

-Increasing the number of pixels allows more fine details to be represented, but also increases the amount of uncompressed data when the color depth stays the same.

-Enlarging a low-resolution raster image does not create the original missing details and may make individual pixels visible (pixelation).

## 6.2 Color Depth (Bit Depth)

-the number of bits used to represent the color of one pixel.

-With n bits per pixel, an image can represent up to 2^n different color values in a direct indexed representation.

Eg: 1 bit per pixel → 2 possible values; 8 bits → 256 possible values; 24 bits → 16,777,216 possible colors.

-A greater color depth allows more colors or tonal levels, which can make gradients look smoother.

-However, more bits per pixel also require more storage for an uncompressed image of the same resolution.

## 6.3 RGB Color Model

-stands for **Red, Green and Blue**.

an additive color model used by many digital displays.

Each pixel color is formed by combining different intensities of red, green and blue light.

-In a common 24-bit RGB image, each channel uses 8 bits and can take a value from 0 to 255. Together, the three channels use 24 bits for each pixel.

Eg: (255, 0, 0) = red; (0, 255, 0) = green; (0, 0, 255) = blue; (0, 0, 0) = black; (255, 255, 255) = white; (255, 255, 0) = yellow.

## 6.4 Image File Size

-For an uncompressed raster image with a fixed number of bits per pixel, the basic pixel-data size is calculated by multiplying its width, height and color depth.

Image size (bits) = Width (pixels) × Height (pixels) × Bits per pixel

Image size (bytes) = Width × Height × Bits per pixel ÷ 8 (bits per byte)

Eg: A 800 × 600 image with a color depth of 24 bits requires 800 × 600 × 24 = 11,520,000 bits = 1,440,000 bytes (about 1.44 MB in decimal units) for its raw pixel data.

## 6.5 Bitmap (Raster) and Vector Images

- **Bitmap or raster** images represent pictures using a grid of pixels.

suitable for photographs and detailed color variations, but scaling them up beyond their original resolution may cause pixelation.

Common raster formats include BMP, PNG and JPEG.

- **Vector** images represent shapes through mathematical descriptions such as points, lines, curves and fills instead of storing each display pixel individually.

-They can be resized without the same pixelation problem, making them suitable for logos, diagrams and icons. SVG is a common vector format.

-Note that image representation and image compression are different concepts. Raster images may be stored with either lossless compression (for example PNG) or lossy compression (for example JPEG). Compression is explained in Section 7.

**7. Compression**

-The process of representing data using **fewer bits** by removing redundancy or discarding selected information. It reduces the storage space required for files and the amount of data transmitted over a network.

-There are two main types of compression: lossless compression and lossy compression.

Compression ratio measures how much smaller a file becomes after compression:

**Compression Ratio** = Original Size / Compressed Size

Eg: A 20 MB file compressed to 5 MB has a compression ratio of 20 / 5 = 4:1.

-A higher ratio indicates a larger reduction in size, but it does not necessarily mean a better result:

-lossy compression must also be judged by the quality of the reconstructed data. Actual ratios depend on the content and encoding settings.

# S1M-4 7.1 Lossless Compression

## 7.1 Lossless Compression

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

reduces the size of data without losing any information.

-After decompression, the recovered data is exactly identical to the original, bit for bit. Therefore, the process is **reversible**.

-Lossless compression is suitable for text files, source code, databases and other data in which even a single incorrect character may change the meaning.

-Common lossless formats include ZIP, GZIP, PNG and FLAC.

## 7.1.1 Run-Length Encoding (RLE)

-Run-Length Encoding (RLE) is a **lossless** compression method that replaces consecutive repeated values with a count-value pair. A run is a sequence of the same value appearing one after another.

-To compress data using RLE, read the values from left to right, count how many consecutive times each value appears, then store the count together with the value. During decompression, repeat each value according to its count.

Eg: AAAAABBBCCDAA → 5A3B2C1D2A

Original: 13 characters × 8 bits = 104 bits

Encoded: 10 characters × 8 bits = 80 bits (assuming one digit and one letter per run)

-RLE works best for data containing long runs of **identical values**, such as simple graphics, large areas of one color and some fax images. It is not suitable for frequently changing data: ABCDE → 1A1B1C1D1E, which increases the length from 5 to 10 characters in this simple representation.

-For images, RLE may encode a row of pixels as consecutive color-count pairs. For example, 4 white pixels followed by 3 green pixels can be represented as 4White3Green. Practical encoders must also define how counts and values are separated and represented.

## 7.1.2 Keyword Encoding

-Keyword encoding is a **lossless text** **compression** method that replaces frequently repeated words or strings with shorter symbols or codes. The encoder stores a **substitution dictionary** that maps each code back to its original word or string.

-First, identify repeated strings. Next, assign each selected string a shorter code and replace its occurrences. Finally, store the dictionary with the compressed data so that decompression can restore the original text exactly.

Eg:

Original: the cat and the dog and the bird

Let the → # and → @

Encoded text: # cat @ # dog @ # bird

-However, the dictionary also occupies space, so keyword encoding only reduces the total file size when the savings from substitutions exceed the cost of storing the dictionary and other metadata.

-The code symbols must be distinguishable from ordinary text. Otherwise, a symbol originally present in the text could be confused with a substitution code, making exact decompression impossible.

## 7.1.3 Huffman Coding

-Huffman coding is a **lossless compression** algorithm developed by David Huffman in 1952.

-It assigns shorter binary codes to more frequent symbols and longer codes to less frequent symbols, reducing the total number of bits required.

-Its codes are **prefix-free**: no complete code is the beginning of another complete code. This property allows decoding without ambiguity.

-To construct a Huffman tree

- Count the frequency of each symbol.
- Create one leaf node for each symbol, repeatedly combine the two nodes with the lowest frequencies, and continue until only one tree remains.
- Assign 0 and 1 to the two branches at each split. The path from the root to each symbol determines its binary code.

(S: symbol, F: frequency, L: length, N: number, CW: code word)

## 7.2 Lossy Compression

-Lossy compression reduces file size by permanently discarding some information.

-The decompressed file is an approximation of the original and cannot always be reconstructed exactly. The process is therefore **irreversible**.

Lossy compression is commonly used for photographs, music and videos because small changes in color, detail or sound may be difficult for people to notice. Typical formats and codecs include JPEG, MP3, AAC, H.264 and H.265.

Lossy methods often achieve smaller files than lossless methods for the same source, but greater compression usually reduces quality. Repeatedly saving a file in a lossy format may introduce additional distortion.

## 7.2.1 JPEG

JPEG is a lossy image compression method for continuous-tone pictures, especially photographs with smooth color changes. JPEG stores the image as a compressed representation rather than preserving every original pixel value exactly.

The JPEG compression process can be explained using these main stages:

1. Color space conversion: Convert the image from RGB to a representation such as YCbCr, separating brightness (luminance) from color information (chrominance).

2. Chroma downsampling: Optionally store the color channels at a lower spatial resolution, since the human eye cannot perceive the difference.

3. Split into 8 × 8 blocks: Divide image components into small blocks so each block can be processed separately.

4. Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT): Convert the pixel values into frequency coefficients.

5. Quantization: Divide the frequency coefficients by the selected quantization values and round the results. This step discards precision and is the main irreversible stage of JPEG compression.

6. Entropy encoding: Arrange and encode the quantized values (use RLE / Huffman).

At high compression levels, visible artifacts may appear, including block boundaries, blurred details and ringing around sharp edges. JPEG is effective for photographs, but may be less suitable for text, logos or diagrams with sharp lines, where a lossless format such as PNG may preserve the details better.

# S1M-5 8.1 Data Types and Expressions

## 8.1 Data Types and Expressions

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

A data type describes the **kind** of value. Values that look similar may have different types:

1 is an integer, 1.0 is a float, and "1" is a string.

| **Python type** | **Meaning** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| int | Whole numbers | 0, -2, 29 |
| float | Floating-point numbers | 1.0, 9.902, 1e10, 44e-2 |
| str | Text enclosed in quotation marks | "the", "1", "num of line" |
| bool | Boolean truth values | True, False |

An expression combines values, variables and operators and evaluates to a result. For example, 2 + 3 * 4 evaluates to 14, while age >= 18 evaluates to a Boolean value.

String concatenation uses + to join strings: "a" + "b" gives "ab". String repetition uses * with an integer: "ab" * 3 gives "ababab". Convert numbers with str() before concatenating them with strings.

**Variables and assignment**

A variable name refers to a value that can be used later. Python creates a variable when a value is first assigned to its name. Assignment evaluates the right-hand expression first and then binds the left-hand name to the result. = assigns a value; == compares values.

spam = 42
x = y = z = 50 # one value assigned to three names
a, b, c = 5, 10, 15 # corresponding values assigned
x = x + 2 # use the old x, then update x
print((a==b, y==z)) # (False, True)

For the names used in this course, use letters, digits and underscores. Begin with a letter or underscore, never a digit. Spaces and punctuation such as -, !, @ and . are not allowed. Names are case sensitive: age, Age and AGE are different. Reserved keywords such as if, for, True and False cannot be variable names. Examples: cake_count and _total are valid; 8piece and number of cakes are invalid.

## 8.2 Input Output and Common Functions

print() displays values. input() reads a line and returns a string, even when the user types digits. Use int(), float() and str() to convert values when needed. Converting unsuitable text, such as int("apple"), raises an error.

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
ph = float(input("Enter the pH level: "))
print("Age:", age)
print("Next year: " + str(age + 1))

String methods are called on a string, for example text.upper(). They return a result without changing the original string. lower() converts letters to lowercase; upper() converts letters to uppercase.

| **Method** | **Meaning** | **Example result** |
|---|---|---|
| s.isalnum() | Nonempty string containing only letters and/or digits | "A12" -> True |
| s.isdigit() | Nonempty string containing only digit characters | "123" -> True; "-3" -> False |
| s.isalpha() | Nonempty string containing only letters | "Hello" -> True; "Hi2" -> False |

+ Spaces make these tests False.

words = input().split() # e.g. "12 7 3" -> ["12", "7", "3"]
nums = []
for word in words:
 nums.append(int(word)) # [12, 7, 3]

## 8.3 Operators and Precedence

**Arithmetic and relational operators**

| **Symbol** | **Meaning** | **Example** | **Result** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ** | Exponentiation | 2 ** 3 | 8 |
| % | Remainder | 22 % 8 | 6 |
| // | Floor division | 22 // 8 | 2 |
| / | Division | 22 / 8 | 2.75 |
| * | Multiplication | 3 * 5 | 15 |
|  | Subtraction | 5 - 2 | 3 |
| + | Addition | 5 + 2 | 7 |

Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 // 2 is -4. / produces a float for integer operands: 6 / 2 is 3.0. ** means power; ^ is not the power operator in Python (note that int() is another method to floor a float value; e.g. int(8.7) == 8 returns True).

| **Symbol** | **Meaning** | **Example** | **Result** |
|---|---|---|---|
| < | Less than | 2 ** 3 < 9 | True |
| > | Greater than | 0 > 1 | False |
| <= | Less than or equal to | 4 <= 5 | True |
| >= | Greater than or equal to | 9 ** 0.5 >= 3 | True |
| == | Equal to | 1 == 2 | False |
| != | Not equal to | "B" != "B" | False |

**Boolean operators and truth table**

For Boolean operands, and returns True only when both operands are True; or returns True when at least one operand is True; not reverses a Boolean value.

| **A** | **B** | **A and B** | **A or B** | **not A** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| True | True | True | True | False |
| True | False | False | True | False |
| False | True | False | True | True |
| False | False | False | False | True |

Common precedence from highest to lowest: ** > *,/,//,% > -,+ > in > not > and > or. Parentheses make the intended order explicit.

2 + 2 == 4 and not 2 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2
#True and not False and True -> True
not 2 > 1 and 3 < 4 or 5 > 5 and 2 > 1 and 3 >= 3
#(not True and True) or (False and True and True) -> False

Augmented assignment combines an operation with assignment. For numeric values, x += 2 corresponds to x = x + 2. There’s also -=, *=, /=, //= and %=, corresponding to subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division and remainder followed by assignment.

## 8.4 Selection Statements

**The if statement**

An if block runs only when its condition is True. Separate if statements are checked independently, so several blocks may run, or none may run.

ph = float(input("Enter the pH level: "))
if ph < 7.0:
 print(ph, "is acidic.")
if ph > 7.0:
 print(ph, "is alkaline.")
#At pH 7.0, neither block prints a message.

**The if else statement**

if and else provide two alternatives. Exactly one block runs when execution reaches this structure.

n = int(input())
line = "Today, I ate " + str(n) + " apple"
if n > 1:
 line = line + "s."
else:
 line = line + "."
print(line)

**The if elif else statement**

Conditions are checked from top to bottom. Only the first True branch runs. The else block handles all remaining cases. Order matters: a broad condition placed first can prevent later branches from running.

age = int(input("What is your age? "))
if age < 11:
 print("You are a kid.")
elif age < 20:
 print("You are a teenager.")
else:
 print("You are an adult.")

## 8.5 Lists and List Operations

A list is an ordered, mutable collection. Use square brackets with comma-separated elements, or use list() to build a list from an iterable.

Python list indices start at 0. len(lst) counts elements; for a nonempty list, the last positive index is len(lst) - 1, and lst[-1] accesses the last element. An index outside the available positions raises IndexError.

| **Operation** | **Effect** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| lst[i] | Read the element at index i | [10, 20, 30][1] gives 20 |
| lst[i] = value | Replace an existing element | nums[1] = 10 |
| lst.append(value) | Add one element at the end | nums.append(12) |
| lst.insert(i, value) | Insert before index i; later items shift right | nums.insert(2, 12) |
| del lst[i] | Delete by index; later items shift left | del nums[2] |
| lst.remove(value) | Delete the first matching value | [1, 3, 3] becomes [1, 3] |
| lst.index(value) | Return the index of the first match | [1, 3, 5, 7, 9].index(7) gives 3 |

remove() and index() raise ValueError if the value is absent. Methods such as append(), insert() and remove() change the list in place and return None. Write nums.append(12), rather than nums = nums.append(12).

nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums[1] = 10 # [0, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5]
nums.append(12) # [0, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
nums.insert(2, 99) # [0, 10, 99, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
del nums[2] # [0, 10, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
nums = [1, 5, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3]
nums.remove(3) # [1, 5, 4, 2, 0, 3]

## 8.6 For Loops and While Loops

**For loops and range**

A for loop visits each item of an iterable, such as a list, string or range. It is convenient for traversing a collection or repeating a known number of times.

range(stop) starts at 0. range(start, stop) uses a step of 1. range(start, stop, step) uses the given step. The start is included and the stop is excluded. A negative step counts down; a step of zero is invalid.

list(range(5)) # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
list(range(2, 8, 2)) # [2, 4, 6]
list(range(5, 0, -1)) # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
nList = []
for i in range(2, 120, 3):
 nList.append(i)
#2, 5, ..., 119: (119 - 2) // 3 + 1 = 40 elements

**While loops**

A while loop checks its condition before every iteration and repeats while the condition remains True. It may run zero times. It is useful when the stopping condition is known but the required number of iterations is not. Update the variables controlling the condition to avoid an infinite loop.

i, total = 1, 0
n = int(input("Enter n: "))
while i <= n:
 total += i
 i += 1
print(total) # n = 5 gives 15

## 8.7 String Operations

**Indexing length and membership**

Strings are ordered sequences of characters. Indexing starts at 0 and negative indices count from the end. With text = "Hello World!", text[0] is "H", text[4] is "o", text[-1] is "!", and len(text) is 12. Strings are immutable, so text[0] = "h" is invalid.

in checks membership and not in checks absence. For strings, membership tests whether a substring occurs: "+" in "1+2" is True and "cat" not in "dog" is True. For lists, membership compares the requested value with the elements: 3 in [1, 3, 5] is True.

**Slicing**

s[start:stop] returns a new string from start up to, but excluding, stop. Omitting start uses the beginning; omitting stop uses the end. For s = "python":

s = "python"
s[:-1] # "pytho"
s[-1:] # "n"
s[1:] # "ython"
s[:1] # "p"
s[1:4] # "yth"

In s[start:stop:step], the third value, step, controls how far the index moves each time.

- A positive step moves forward.
- A negative step moves backward.
- The default step is 1. A step of 0 raises ValueError.

s = "python"
s[::1] # "python" — every character
s[::2] # "pto" — every second character
s[1::2] # "yhn" — every second character, starting at index 1
s[::-1] # "nohtyp" — reverse the string
s[::-2] # "nhy" — every second character, moving backward

**strip and case conversion**

s.strip() removes whitespace only from the beginning and end, including spaces, tabs and newlines. s.strip(chars) removes any of the supplied characters repeatedly from both ends. The argument is a set of removable characters, rather than one exact prefix or suffix. Interior characters remain.

" Hello World! ".strip() # "Hello World!"
"abbaHelloabba".strip("ab") # "Hello"
"Hello".lower() # "hello"
"Hello".upper() # "HELLO"
"hello".title() # "Hello"

**split and join**

s.split() separates text on runs of whitespace and ignores leading/trailing whitespace. s.split(delimiter) separates on the exact delimiter string and returns a list of strings. With an explicit delimiter, consecutive delimiters can produce empty strings.

" red blue ".split() # ["red", "blue"]
"MyABnameABisABJohn".split("AB") # ["My", "name", "is", "John"]
"a,,b".split(",") # ["a", "", "b"]
url = "http://cn.shsid.org/img/admission_btn.png"
url.split("/")[-1].split(".")[0] # "admission_btn"

delimiter.join(iterable) joins string elements with the delimiter between them and returns one string. The elements must be strings. Passing a string as the iterable joins its individual characters.

" ".join(["My", "name", "is", "John"]) # "My name is John"
".".join(["192", "168", "0", "1"]) # "192.168.0.1"
"-".join("hello") # "h-e-l-l-o"

## 8.8 Nested Loops

A nested loop places one loop inside another. For each outer-loop iteration, the inner loop runs through its iterations. If the outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs m times each time, the inner body executes n × m times. When the inner range depends on the outer variable, count the iterations for each row separately.

## 8.9 Functions Parameters and Return Values

Built-in functions, such as range() and print(), are already available in Python. User-defined functions package code for a specific task. Function abstraction lets the caller use a function by knowing its purpose, inputs and result without needing its internal implementation. Reuse also avoids repeated code.

**Definition and call**

A definition begins with def, a valid function name and parentheses containing any parameters. End the header with a colon and indent the body consistently. Function names follow the same naming rules as variables. A triple-quoted string at the start of the body is a docstring describing the function.

def convert_to_celsius(fahrenheit):
 """Convert a Fahrenheit temperature to Celsius."""
 return (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9

result = convert_to_celsius(80)
print(result) # approximately 26.6667

Parameters are the names in a function definition, such as fahrenheit. Arguments are the actual values supplied at a call, such as 80. Defining a function does not execute its body. At the call, arguments bind to parameters, the body runs, and execution continues at the caller when the function returns.

**Return behavior**

return expression sends a value back to the caller and immediately ends that function call. A function can contain several return statements in different branches, but only one is reached during a particular call. Reaching the end without a return statement, or using a bare return, returns None.

def div(num1, num2):
 if num2 == 0:
 return "Divisor cannot be zero!"
 else:
 return num1 / num2

print(div(6, 2)) # 3.0
print(div(1, 0)) # Divisor cannot be zero!

print() displays output; return supplies a result that another expression can use.

## 8.10 Scope Mutability and Parameter Passing

Python passes object references to functions by assignment. The parameter initially refers to the same object as the argument. Rebinding the parameter changes its local name; mutating a shared mutable object can affect the caller. The PPT labels these examples as passing by value and passing by reference; use the distinction between rebinding and mutation to predict Python behavior.

In python, all variables are references to an object. (You won’t be tested on this but useful to know) However, different types of variables have different behaviors.

**Global variables & Local variables**

Local variables are names created inside a function and accessible within that function. A local name can refer to a mutable object shared with the caller.

Global variables are created outside a function. They are accessible globally, whether from inside a function or not.

Assigning to a name inside a function normally makes it local, even if the same name exists globally. Declare the name global when the function needs to reassign the module-level variable.

x = 10 # globaldef f(): x = 20 # local — shadows the global xf()print(x) # 10 (the global x is unchanged)x = 10 # globaldef f(): x = 20 # local — shadows the global xf()print(x) # 10 (the global x is unchanged)To assign to the module-level name from inside a function, write **global** **x** before the assignment.

x = 10def f(): global x x = 20f()print(x) # 20 (x is changed)x = 10def f(): global x x = 20f()print(x) # 20 (x is changed)

**Immutable types**

int, str, float, bool and tuple are immutable types. None is the single value of the immutable NoneType.

These types are unchangeable. Any modifications to these types will create a new object and bind the variable name to this new object

a = 3

a = 4

Consider this section of code. Python creates an object that has a value of 3 and type of int. Then, python binds the variable name “a” to this object. When “a = 4” is executed, Python creates a new object with type int and value 4. Then, Python binds the variable name “a” to this object.

Assigning a new value to a parameter referring to an immutable object rebinds the local parameter. **The caller’s original binding is unchanged.**

def f(x):x+=1 #local xx = 10 # global xf(x)print(x)def f(x):x+=1 #local xx = 10 # global xf(x)print(x)

**Mutable Types**

List, dictionary, set are mutable types.

Mutable objects can be changed in place by operations such as append(). if you did not want

When a function mutates a mutable object passed as an argument, the caller can observe the change to that shared object.

def f(lst):
lst.append(4)x = [1, 2, 3] # global x
f(x)
print(x) # [1, 2, 3, 4]def f(lst):
lst.append(4)x = [1, 2, 3] # global x
f(x)
print(x) # [1, 2, 3, 4]

Terms to remember:

System unit: The main enclosure of a computer, containing components such as the motherboard, processor, memory, power supply and internal storage devices.

Keyboard: Primary input device

Mouse: A pointing device used to move the pointer and select/interact with items in a graphical user interface (GUI).

Disk: A circular storage medium that holds data magnetically or optically. Examples include the magnetic disks inside a hard drive and optical discs such as CDs and DVDs.

Hard drive: A storage device that uses magnetic disks to store programs and data, retaining them when the power is off.

Optical drive: A device that reads data from optical discs, such as CDs, DVDs or Blu-ray discs. Some models can also write data to compatible discs.

Floppy disk drive: An older storage device that reads and writes data on removable magnetic floppy disks, which have a low storage capacity.

Sound system: The hardware that processes and outputs audio. A sound card or integrated audio circuitry converts digital audio into analog signals for speakers or headphones.

Display system: The hardware that produces visual output. Graphics hardware processes image data, while a monitor or other display presents the resulting images.

Peripheral device: A device connected to a computer to provide input, output or additional storage, such as a keyboard, printer or external drive.

# S1M-7 12.1 Programs and source code

## 12.1 Programs and source code

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Computer programmers create programs that control digital devices. They usually write these programs in a high-level programming language. The human-readable version of a program is called source code.

A processor executes machine-language instructions represented by 0s and 1s. A compiler or interpreter translates the source program into operations the processor can execute. Translation involves expressing the program using the processor's instruction set, rather than simply replacing each source-code character with its binary character code.

| **Feature** | **Compiler** | **Interpreter** |
|---|---|---|
| Translation | Translates the whole source program before it runs. | Translates and executes one statement at a time in the lesson's simplified model. |
| Output | Produces object code that can be saved and used in a later execution. | Does not save a separate translated machine-code program in this model. |
| Running a program | Two stages: translate the program, then execute the resulting code. | Translation and execution proceed together. |
| Main advantage | After translation, execution is generally faster. | Supports convenient development, testing and correction of code. |
| Different platforms | Generated machine code depends on the target platform. | Source can run on another platform with a suitable interpreter and required support. |

## 12.2 Instruction sets and machine language

A processor is an integrated circuit designed to process instructions. A microprocessor implements this circuitry on a chip, typically made using silicon. These chips and other components connect through the system board.

An instruction set is the collection of machine instructions a processor can execute directly. Simple operations include addition, subtraction, counting and comparison. These operations can be combined to carry out many different tasks, making the processor general purpose.

A machine-language instruction has two parts:

| **Part** | **Meaning** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Opcode | Operation code that tells the processor which action to perform. | MOV |
| Operand | The value, register or memory location used by the operation. | AL, 34h (AL is an IR, while 34h is a hexadecimal val) |

These bit patterns are an example encoding for the lesson, rather than a universal encoding used by every processor.

## 12.3 Processor logic and registers

In a stored-program model, program instructions and data are loaded into main memory (RAM) from input or secondary storage before execution. The CPU works with memory to process input and produce output. Secondary storage retains programs and data between uses.

The CPU contains a control unit (CU), an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), and registers. Registers are small, fast temporary storage locations used for instructions, data and intermediate results.

| **Component or register** | **Role** |
|---|---|
| Control unit (CU) | Uses control signals to coordinate instruction execution and direct data between memory, registers, the ALU and other system components. |
| Arithmetic logic unit (ALU) | Performs arithmetic, such as addition and subtraction, and logical operations, such as comparing two values. |
| Program counter (PC) | Holds the memory address of the next instruction to fetch. |
| Instruction register (IR) | Holds the fetched instruction while the CPU decodes and executes it. |
| General purpose registers | Hold operands and intermediate values during processing. |
| Accumulator | In the lesson's example, holds an ALU result before it is used again or transferred to memory. |

The CU fetches the instruction from the address in the PC into the IR and updates the PC for the following instruction. The ALU performs the required calculation when directed by the CU.

## 12.4 The machine instruction cycle

A machine cycle, also called an instruction cycle, is the process of fetching and carrying out one machine instruction. It include four stages:

| **Stage** | **What happens** | **Timing group** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Fetch | The CU retrieves the next instruction from memory and places it in the IR. | Instruction time (I-time) |
| 2 Decode | The CU interprets the opcode and identifies the operands or required data locations. | Instruction time (I-time) |
| 3 Execute | The required data is moved into registers. The ALU performs an arithmetic or logical operation when needed. | Execution time (E-time) |
| 4 Store | The result is written to a register or memory for later use, output or permanent storage. | Execution time (E-time) |

Instruction time + execution time = one machine instruction cycle. An instruction cycle can span multiple clock cycles.

Example: to add 4 and 5 and save the result, the CU fetches and decodes the instruction, arranges for the operands to reach registers, signals the ALU to calculate 9, and stores the result. The CU coordinates these steps; the ALU carries out the arithmetic.

# S1M-8 13.1 Random access memory

## 13.1 Random access memory

> From the Grade 10 Resource Department's Semester 1 Midterm Computer Science AP review guide (PA). Writers: Summer Liang 10-4, Forrest Yan 10-8. Editor: Caitlin Zhou 10-2, Rick Yu 10-12. Range: ALL. Student-made reference material: where it differs from class, follow class.

Random access memory (RAM) is the computer's working memory. It holds instructions and data for programs in use, raw data waiting to be processed, and results waiting to be output or saved.

RAM acts as a waiting room for the processor. The CU coordinates movement of instructions and data between RAM and the CPU. After processing, results can return to RAM until they are needed again or sent to an output or storage device.

RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when power is removed. Secondary storage retains data without continuous power and usually offers greater capacity. Saving a file copies data from working memory to persistent storage.

In dynamic RAM (DRAM), microscopic capacitors represent bits using charge. In the lesson's model, a charged capacitor represents 1 and a discharged capacitor represents 0. Eight bits form one byte, and memory locations have addresses. The charge must be refreshed to retain the data.

| **RAM measure** | **Meaning and example** |
|---|---|
| Capacity in GB | The amount of data RAM can hold. More capacity allows larger programs and more data to remain in working memory, up to the computer's supported limit. |
| Frequency in MHz | Millions of cycles per second. Under comparable conditions, a higher rating indicates faster operation. |
| Access time in ns | Time taken to respond. One nanosecond is one billionth of a second; lower is faster |

## 13.2 Types of RAM

| **Feature** | **SRAM** | **DRAM** |
|---|---|---|
| Full name | Static random access memory | Dynamic random access memory |
| Data retention while powered | Holds its state without periodic refresh. | Stores charge that must be refreshed. |
| Typical access speed | Faster | Slower |
| Storage density | Lower density; usually smaller capacity for a comparable chip area. | Higher density; suitable for larger memory capacity. |
| Cost for a comparable capacity | More expensive | Less expensive |
| Power loss | Data is lost. | Data is lost. |

SDRAM means synchronous dynamic random access memory. It coordinates memory operations with a clock to improve the interface between the memory and its controller. DDR memory is a family of synchronous DRAM. DDR generations include DDR, DDR2, DDR3 and DDR4; different generations are not interchangeable and must match the system's supported memory type.

## 13.3 Virtual memory

When programs need more working space than the available RAM can provide, the operating system can use part of secondary storage as virtual memory. It keeps some program or data portions there and brings them back into RAM when needed.

Virtual memory allows the computer to handle a larger working set, but frequent movement between storage and RAM reduces performance because secondary storage is slower. Adding compatible RAM, within the system's limits, can reduce reliance on virtual memory.

## 13.4 ROM and the startup process

Read only memory (ROM) is nonvolatile memory (it retains its contents without power).

The BIOS(Basic Input Output System) startup model performs internal hardware checks and starts the process of finding the operating system and loading its kernel from storage into RAM. The kernel is the central part of the operating system; loading and starting the operating system is called bootstrapping, or booting.

Startup sequence: power on -> run BIOS firmware and check hardware -> locate the operating system on storage -> load the kernel into RAM -> begin operating system control.

| **Memory type** | **Main property** |
|---|---|
| MROM(Mask ROM) | Programmed during manufacture and read only in normal use. |
| PROM(Programmable ROM) | Can be programmed once. |
| EPROM(Erasable PROM) | Can be erased and programmed again. |
| EEPROM (Electrically EPROM) | Can be erased and reprogrammed electrically. |
| Flash memory | Nonvolatile memory that can be electrically erased and rewritten. It retains stored data without power. |

## 13.5 Cache and the memory hierarchy

Cache is a relatively small, very fast memory used to speed up access to instructions and data. Keeping useful items close to the CPU reduces the time spent fetching them from slower main memory. Cache commonly has levels called L1, L2 and L3.

The main working-data hierarchy is registers, then cache, then RAM, then secondary storage. Registers and cache provide fast access with small capacity. RAM provides more working space. Secondary storage retains larger amounts of data between uses. Virtual memory uses secondary storage under operating system control.

| **Storage area** | **Primary purpose** | **Retains data without power** |
|---|---|---|
| Registers | Operands, instructions and intermediate results inside the CPU. | No |
| Cache | Fast access to data and instructions near the CPU. | No |
| RAM | Working instructions and data for active programs. | No |
| ROM or flash firmware | Persistent startup instructions. | Yes |
| Secondary storage | Longer term storage of programs and files. | Yes |

## 13.6 Factors affecting CPU performance

CPU performance depends on clock speed, data transfer, cache, word size, instruction set, core count and how instructions are scheduled.

| **Factor** | **Meaning** **&** **effect** **& notes** |
|---|---|
| Clock speed | The clock sets the pace of processor activity. |
| Instructions per cycle | Clock speed is not the same as instructions per second. Some instructions take several cycles, while some processors complete more than one instruction in a cycle. |
| Front side bus (FSB) | FSB carries data to and from the processor. A faster bus can reduce delays in data transfer. Its frequency is expressed in MHz. |
| Cache | A small, fast memory that can reduce time waiting for instructions and data from RAM. |
| Word size | The number of bits the processor can manipulate at one time. A larger word allows it to handle more bits in an operation. |
| Instruction set | Determines the machine operations available and how a task is expressed as instructions. |
| Multiple cores | Multiple cores can work on separate tasks or portions of a task when the software supports this. |

## 13.7 RISC and CISC instruction sets

| **Feature** | **RISC** | **CISC** |
|---|---|---|
| Full name | Reduced instruction set computing | Complex instruction set computing |
| General approach | Emphasizes simpler instructions. | Includes more complex instructions. |
| Cycles and task length | use fewer cycles but more instructions. | perform more work but require several cycles. |
| Traditional design tradeoff | Simpler instruction execution logic. | More complex execution logic, with potential power costs. |

The distinction between RISC and CISC have become less clear as implementations have evolved.

## 13.8 Pipelining and parallel processing

Pipelining overlaps the stages of different instructions. While one instruction is executing, another can be decoding and a later one can be fetched. The next instruction can begin before the previous instruction has completed every stage. This improves the rate at which instructions move through the processor.

Without pipelining, instruction 1 completes fetch, decode, execute and store before instruction 2 begins. With pipelining, different instructions occupy different stages at the same time.

Parallel processing uses multiple processors or processing cores at the same time. A task therefore can be divided into parts, processed concurrently and have its results combined. Pipelining overlaps instruction stages, while parallel processing performs work across multiple processing units.

## 13.9 Overclocking

Overclocking increases the operating speed of a component beyond its normal rated setting. However, it also can cause overheating and unreliable operation.
